syllabusTopics: IUPAC Nomenclature of Organic Compounds (up to chain having 6-carbon atoms)
Qualitative analysis of organic compounds (detection of N, S and halogens by Lassaigne's test)

Structural isomerism and its types: chain isomerism, position isomerism, functional isomerism, metamerism and tautomerism
Concept of geometrical isomerism (cis and trans) and optical isomerism (d and l form)
Preliminary idea of reaction mechanism: homolytic and heterolytic fission

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Organic reagents come in three classes. **Electrophiles** are **electron-deficient** — charged (H⁺, NO₂⁺, CH₃⁺) or neutral (BF₃, AlCl₃, SO₃ with incomplete octets) — and attack **electron-rich** sites: π bonds and lone pairs. **Nucleophiles** are **electron-rich** — charged (OH⁻, CN⁻, Cl⁻) or neutral (H₂O, NH₃, ROH via lone pairs) — and donate a pair to **electron-poor** centres; electrophile and nucleophile are…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - Electrophiles: H⁺, NO₂⁺, CH₃⁺, Br⁺, BF₃, AlCl₃, SO₃ - Nucleophiles: OH⁻, CN⁻, Cl⁻, CH₃O⁻, H₂O, NH₃, ROH - Radical chain: Cl₂ → 2Cl·; Cl· + CH₄ → CH₃· + HCl; CH₃· + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl·; Cl· + Cl· → Cl₂

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Covers only: electrophiles, nucleophiles, free-radicals (within Fundamental Principles of Organic Chemistry).  ·  Out of scope here: topics of neighbouring units in Chemistry — don't mix them.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: "Electrophiles are electron-deficient species attacking electron-rich centres; nucleophiles are electron-rich species donating a pair to electron-deficient centres; free radicals are neutral species with unpaired electrons."

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***The neutral electrophile*** — BF3 has no charge but an empty p orbital; it grabs electron pairs as eagerly as any cation — deficiency, not charge, defines the family.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — The Three Attackers Once fission has made an electron-hungry or electron-rich species, reactions are a matter of matching attacker to target. **Electrophiles** love electrons and attack electron-rich sites; **nucleophiles** love nuclei (positive centres) and donate electron pairs; **free radicals** carry unpaired electrons and strip atoms from bonds.…  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 Electrophiles (E⁺) - **Definition:** electron-loving species — **electron-deficient**, accept an electron pair; attack **electron-rich** sites (double bonds, lone pairs). - **Charged:** H⁺, NO₂⁺ (nitronium), CH₃⁺ (carbocation), Br⁺, Cl⁺. - **Neutral:** BF₃, AlCl₃, SO₃ — incomplete octets or polarised atoms make them acceptors.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: E+ attacks electron-rich (π, lone pairs); Nu− donates to δ+ C; radical = neutral 7e from homolysis. Charged + neutral examples for each: H+/BF3; OH−/NH3; Cl·. Chain steps: initiation, propagation, termination.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Match attacker to target: electrophiles find π bonds and lone pairs, nucleophiles find δ+ carbons, radicals strip hydrogens — identify the reagent class and the reaction predicts itself.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Electrophile: electron-deficient, accepts pair, attacks electron-rich sites; charged H+, NO2+, CH3+, Br+; neutral BF3, AlCl3, SO3 (incomplete octet). Nucleophile: electron-rich, donates pair, attacks electron-deficient centres; charged OH-, CN-, Cl-, CH3O-; neutral H2O, NH3, ROH (lone pairs).…

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Radical chain reactions run the world's plastics: ethene polymerises by radical initiation, each propagation step adding another monomer to the growing chain.
